articles.title: We discovered an organism that lives at blistering temperatures – but what allows it to take the heat?
articles.author: Kristen Skruber, Assistant Professor of Biology, Gonzaga University
paras: Organisms are products of the environments they live and evolve in. While the physical world is governed by universal laws like thermodynamics and gravity, there are few laws of biology. An open question for biologists like me is how environmental conditions shape what organisms look like and dictate how they live, breathe and move.

Organisms can adapt to survive in a wide variety of conditions, from salty water to extreme heat or cold and changing climates. Most eukaryotic organisms that have been studied with cell types similar to our own live at temperatures close to those of the human body, with an average of 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 degrees Celsius).

Organisms thriving at temperatures higher than this range, known as thermophiles, could help directly answer what effect temperature has on the rules for life. These rules can help scientists learn more about where life could exist. In a study published in September 2026, our research team identified a new thermophile that can survive at hotter conditions than any other previously recorded.
Discovering life at a new extreme

Eukaryotic cells, like the ones found in our bodies, contain organelles like nuclei and mitochondria. Eukaryotic organisms are reported less often than bacteria in extreme conditions, and based on observations from fungi at 140 F (60 C), scientists had theorized that eukaryotic life is not physically possible beyond 143 F (62 C).

In our new study, our team isolated and characterized a unicellular eukaryote, Incendiamoeba cascadensis, which is able to reproduce at 145 F (63 C). This finding marks the highest temperature yet recorded for eukaryotic life.
Our team found Incendiamoeba cascadensis in geothermal springs in Lassen Volcanic National Park, in Northern California, but we suspect it might also be found in other geothermal areas worldwide.

Like many amoebae – cells that change shape as they move – Incendiamoeba is a forager. It can move around in search of food and favorable conditions. It actively crawls at 147 F (64 C), but a few degrees more and it will enter a protective hibernation-like state.
What sets thermophiles apart?

While bacteria have been recorded living up to 212 F (100 C), it is unclear why eukaryotic cells are less amenable to high temperatures and other extremes. Many theories abound: Our cells have more protective membranes, including several membranes within each cell, surrounding their organelles. We also have complex molecular machinery that maintains our large genomes, and a dynamic cytoskeleton: a network of proteins that allows our cells to move.

Like other eukaryotes, Incendiamoeba has organelles, an active cytoskeleton and a relatively large genome, so what allows it to persist where others cannot? So far, Incendiamoeba has revealed that we don’t yet know which parts of eukaryotes are generally incompatible with high temperature.

As someone who investigates phenomena at the molecular level, I am always thinking about how molecules move and how motion increases with temperature. At higher temperatures, the velcrolike bonds holding proteins together can unfold, preventing them from performing their vital functions. Eukaryotes have evolved protein helpers called heat shock proteins, which detect protein unfolding and help refold them.

So, could Incendiamoeba simply have more of these helper proteins? Our team found that it does have a large reservoir of heat shock proteins, but making these proteins requires a lot of energy, and they must be folded themselves, so more helper proteins probably isn’t the full answer.

Incendiamoeba also has a unique set of protein building blocks that are good at holding proteins together. Yet this composition may only make up for the fact that proteins degrade more easily with increasing temperature.

We can look at Incendiamoeba’s genes, which turn on – or up – when temperature rises. Many of these genes are unknown. It is possible that one of these mystery genes is the key to its ability to withstand high temperatures. However, it is more likely, and in my mind, much more interesting, that there exists a symphony of small changes this organism has evolved, which confer its unique abilities.
By investigating Incendiamoeba and finding others like it, we can determine those changes and learn about the key principles for how life works on our environmentally diverse planet.
Kristen Skruber receives funding from the M.J. Murdock Charitable Trust.

articles.title: Driverless 18-wheelers are on a few highways, but widespread use is a long way down the road
articles.author: Shannon Roberts, Associate Professor of Industrial Engineering, UMass Amherst
paras: Driverless trucks with artificial intelligence on board could dramatically change the landscape of freight shipping. A few companies have begun testing early models on some limited routes in Texas and California. Simulations of automated fleets show the potential benefits of the technology: The vehicles could improve safety, enhance fuel economy and lessen transit times.

Truck makers and operators still have to solve some major issues, however, including how automated trucks will operate in variable weather and road conditions, and whether drivers should still be inside big rigs.
I am an engineer who studies human factors and transportation safety, and in my view, it is likely that automated trucks and human drivers will be working together for quite some time.

Fully automated trucks, which can drive on an interstate highway in good weather without human intervention, use a combination of AI, machine learning, computer vision, pattern recognition and adaptive decision-making. Torc, one company developing these vehicles, uses AI to combine data from multiple sensors and generate models that predict truck performance.

Data taken from modern big rigs that are equipped with certain technology such as automatic emergency braking and lane-keeping assistance systems indicate that fully automated, driverless trucks could reduce the number and severity of crashes. They could also save fuel and therefore cost by optimizing acceleration and braking, and by running multiple vehicles in a close-knit convoy or platoon. Driverless trucks could reduce parking needs as well as emissions from idling because they could run almost 24 hours a day and would not need to idle when they do park, which is common for regular rigs at truck stops.

Finally, automated trucks could help ease the ongoing driver shortage. Ironically, automation could make driving less stressful and less physically demanding, improving job satisfaction among drivers.
Weather and work zones are hard to navigate
The main reason automated trucks are not common today is that they have difficulty operating in variable weather, under changing roadway conditions and alongside unpredictable drivers.

Automated trucks require sensors, radars and cameras that gather information about the environment around them to make decisions. However, snow and rain remain a problem for all automated vehicles, including cars, because they prevent the technology from “seeing” the roadway. Driverless taxi company Waymo, for example, only operates driverless cars in areas that get no snow.

Furthermore, any stretch of road where there may not be a predictable, clear surface and prevalent lines is difficult to handle. Imagine a construction zone with orange cones, narrow lanes and missing lane lines. Driverless car companies still try to avoid these areas. And, oddly, some research shows that automobile drivers tend to crash into driverless cars at a higher rate than they do cars piloted by people.
Given those challenges, companies are testing automated trucks on roads that lack complications.

For example, autonomous truck maker Aurora is operating large freight trucks on I-45, a relatively flat and straight highway between Dallas and Houston. Rival Kodiak’s robotrucks are delivering sand to industrial sites in Texas over roads few people use. Few if any automated trucks are being tested in chaotic urban environments, given the pedestrians, bicyclists, traffic lights and elements of city traffic.
Some companies that were developing automated trucks have scaled back ambitions, changed direction or exited the market.

In 2023, Embark, TuSimple and Locomotion closed down. Waymo began to focus solely on cars. Other companies narrowed their focus to trucks that would operate only along a few dedicated routes between two large cities or manufacturing sites.
Drivers and trucks that work together
In my view, for years to come, automated trucks with AI-based controls will still require a driver.

The best technology will support a symbiosis between human and machine, where the person and the truck each do what they do best. A human would likely drive the truck across the “first mile” – the uncertain and crowded warehouse grounds and local streets to a highway. The driver would then stop using the steering wheel, gas pedal and brake and let automation take over. The human would take back control during the “last mile” to the truck’s final destination.

Research my colleagues and I conducted shows that human-machine interfaces that communicate between drivers and autonomous vehicles will be key. For example, a screen or heads-up display inside the cab would tell the driver how the technology is doing. Verbal messages or a vibrating seat could signal that the automation cannot handle a developing situation, and the driver would take over.

Developers will have to be aware of possible biases. So-called automation bias could lead to a driver who trusts and relies on the truck’s decision-making so much that they defer to it. Algorithmic bias could cause truck sensors to recognize certain groups of people on the road more than others, such as only detecting pedestrians of a certain size or shape.

The long-term vision is to have no driver, in part to lower costs. But driverless trucks do not seem to me to be practical on a large scale in the near future. It is more realistic to envision the driver and the automated truck as a team. Vehicle manufacturers, technology developers, regulators and drivers will need to work together to realize the benefits.

Shannon Roberts receives funding from the Massachusetts Department of Transportation, National Science Foundation, NYSEARCH, Sloan Foundation, and US Department of Transportation. She has previously received funding from Belron, GM, and Toyota Collaborative Safety Research Center.

articles.title: England needs 120% of normal rainfall to come out of drought this winter – storms won’t fix that yet
articles.author: Hannah Cloke, Regius Professor of Meteorology and Climate Science, University of Reading
paras: Storm Austen and Storm Boelo swept across the UK in quick succession. Rain lashed windows, river levels rose and the clocks went back. It feels like winter has arrived all at once.

Yet most of England and Wales are still in drought. Parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset and Sussex are in severe drought, the highest level the Environment Agency can declare. South-west and south-east England have had their driest April to September in over 100 years.

But how can this be when it is cold, dark and pouring with rain? Drought tightens or loosens its grip over months, not just a few days. It will be the rainy or dry nature of the months ahead that will decide whether the drought ends, or more worryingly, if it stays into next summer.
Winter should fill the tank

Summer droughts grab the headlines and public attention. When we have a dry period over the summer it’s everywhere, with brown lawns, hosepipe bans and cracked reservoir beds. But winter is when the UK refills its water stores.

Between October and March, with shorter and colder days, less water evaporates and plants drink far less, so rain finally has the chance to refill our reservoirs. Rain can soak deep into the ground to top up groundwater, the water held in chalk and sandstone rocks beneath our feet, like a giant sponge. Groundwater supplies much of the drinking water in southern and eastern England, but it fills slowly, over months and years.

Think of it like a bank account. A hot summer is a big splurge with lots of withdrawals. But a dry winter means the deposits needed to repay that spending never arrive. That’s why a dry winter can do more damage to our water supplies than a heatwave.

This year the account is badly overdrawn. Southern England has just had its driest April to September in more than a century, alongside record summer heat. The Wimbleball reservoir on Exmoor, which supplies around 400,000 people, was full in March, after an extremely wet winter. Then the weather shifted from wetter than normal to dryer than normal. By October, water levels at Wimbleball were down to about 13%.
How unusual is a winter drought?

Droughts that carry on into winter are rare in the UK. Usually the autumn rain arrives, soil gets wetter and water stores recover by Christmas. Every instinct suggests that a stormy autumn should fix things.

In the 2010 to 2012 drought, two dry winters in a row left groundwater in south and east England so low that hosepipe bans came in during spring 2012. Then the wettest April on record arrived, and parts of the country swung from drought to flood within weeks.
What stands out now is how quickly droughts are stacking up. This is the third drought in England in five years. The stores barely have time to recover before the next one begins.

England and Wales can be in drought and experience flooding simultaneously. After months of dry weather it takes a lot of rain to wet the ground all the way through. Storms such as Boelo and Austen bring bursts of heavy rain. Drains are overwhelmed and rivers rise quickly, sometimes spilling out onto their floodplains. But the reservoirs and groundwater that supply our taps respond far more slowly, and need lots of water to fill up. So the type of winter rains make a big difference.

Floods can hit fast. But the key parts of the water cycle are slow. Rain has to wet the soil all the way through before it can trickle down into the rock, and groundwater can take months to respond. The Environment Agency estimates England needs around 120% of normal rainfall between September and April for every area to come out of drought. We would need half a year with consistently more rain than we would expect at this time of year to break this drought.
If rain falls short across the whole winter, then England could start next summer in drought, with even less room for manoeuvre.
Will winter droughts become more common?

But climate scientists don’t expect there will be a dry winter every year, either now or in decades ahead as fossil fuel burning continues to heat the planet. Climate projections suggest UK winters will get wetter on average. But averages can hide the danger.

Summers heated by the burning of fossil fuels dry out the soil and drain reservoirs faster, leaving a bigger hole for winter to fill. Winter rain is increasingly arriving in heavy bursts that are harder to capture and more likely to flood. And natural swings in the weather will still deliver dry winters from time to time. Put those together and the chance of a drought rolling into winter, or across two winters, goes up. This is a trend that will keep getting worse as long as we keep heating the planet.
Preparing starts with how we think about water. It is precious, not endless. Yet we have built a system that lets a wet winter rush away to the sea, then rations what is left through a dry summer.

As with other parts of the UK’s water system, we are paying the price now for years of chronic underinvestment. Water companies need to move much faster on fixing leaks, which still waste billions of litres every day. New reservoirs are being planned in England, which will help deliver more storage. But they will take more than a decade to build, cost billions of pounds, and cannot be the whole solution.

There is also a low-tech local answer, that would need regulation and a programme of retrofitting to make a big difference. Rainwater harvesting and water reuse in new and existing homes, sustainable drainage in our towns, and encouraging wetlands and floodplains that hold water like a sponge.
Changes to our landscape and homes can help prevent both problems.
Each of us can help. Take shorter showers, ask your water company about a meter and and fit a water butt to catch rain for the garden. These habits add up.
Autumn storms have started to replenish water reserves, but it’s not the finish line. We also need to get ahead of what is likely to happen in years to come.

Hannah Cloke advises the Environment Agency, the European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasts, the Copernicus Emergency Management Service, local and national governments and humanitarian agencies on the forecasting and warning of natural hazards. She is a fellow of the European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasts. Her research is funded by the UKRI Engineering & Physical Sciences Research Council, the UKRI Natural Environment Research Council, the European Commission and the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office.

articles.title: The UK wants ‘AI sovereignty’ to cut its reliance on foreign tech – here’s how that can be achieved
articles.author: Vincent Charles, Professor of AI for Business and Management Science, Queen's University Belfast
paras: The UK government wants to grow the country’s native AI industry to reduce its dependence on systems made by foreign companies.
In the Budget on October 28, Chancellor John Healey announced more money – £60 million – for the national Sovereign AI Fund to support promising UK AI companies.

The government launched the fund in April 2026, committing £500 million at the time to boost the UK’s AI capability. Based in the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), it operates much like a government backed venture capital fund.

But this unit offers more than money. Companies can gain access to some of the UK’s most powerful AI supercomputers, including Isambard-AI, alongside research support and opportunities to work with the government.

The UK government initiatives are part of a wider global push towards sovereign AI. This term refers to countries strengthening their ability to develop and use the AI technologies they rely on while retaining greater control over them. There is concern about the risks of dependence on foreign suppliers – and the potential disruption to UK infrastructure if something were to happen to one of those suppliers.
But what does sovereign AI mean in practice – and can the UK learn anything from what’s going on elsewhere in the world?

For some, sovereignty means controlling everything needed to develop and run AI. For others, it means building domestic AI models or keeping data within national borders. A recent analysis published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace shows how complex this can be.
AI depends on computer chips, data, electricity, skilled workers, internet connections, and cybersecurity. A country may control some of these while depending on foreign suppliers for others.
In practice, four ideas tend to be bundled together. The first is ownership: who owns the chips, data centres, and models? The second is jurisdiction: whose laws apply and where is the data held?

The third is capability: can a country build, adapt, and run AI itself? The fourth is resilience: can essential services continue if a supplier withdraws access? Many disagreements about sovereign AI concern which of these ideas matters most.
The Center for a New American Security (CNAS), a US think tank, tracks government-backed sovereign AI projects. In January 2023, it recorded just one project.

By mid-2026, that number had risen to 184 projects across 67 countries. These figures show how quickly interest in sovereign AI has grown globally. However, they count projects, not whether those projects have succeeded.

Countries are making different choices about where to invest. India, for example, has focused on building domestic computing capacity, promoting the development of AI models and setting up national datasets for “training” AI models. Its IndiaAI Mission has deployed around 38,000 graphics processing units (GPUs) – specialised processors used to develop and run AI – to boost computing power for developers.
Other Indian initiatives include BharatGen AI, a multilingual AI model, and AIKosh, a national platform to provide startups and researchers with access to anonymised training data.

According to the same report by CNAS, most countries focus on just one or two layers of the AI stack – the collection of technologies and infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI systems. Only a handful of jurisdictions, such as India, South Korea, the UK, and Taiwan, have operational programmes covering computing infrastructure, models, and data. Ghana and South Africa, meanwhile, have launched projects focused on expanding domestic AI computing capacity.
Sovereign and also dependent?

While some nations are making strides towards sovereign AI, almost every country relies on foreign AI technology to some extent. Rather than developing models from scratch, many adapt existing – or base – models developed abroad. According to CNAS, around three-fifths of the foreign base models identified in the projects it tracks come from the US.

A 2026 report by researchers from the Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) at Georgetown University, Washington DC, highlights the risks of foreign technology supply chains. Trade restrictions and geopolitical tensions can disrupt access, particularly to advanced computer chips, which are produced by a small number of specialised suppliers. But dependence is not the whole story.

Researchers at Stanford University in California have argued that sovereignty is better understood as managing AI dependencies rather than eliminating them. Their report underlines the fact that supporting domestic companies and adopting open-source technologies can widen the available choices.

Diversifying foreign technology suppliers is another option. For example, the CNAS report identifies projects in Egypt, Singapore, Thailand, Uganda, and the UAE using Alibaba’s Qwen models, developed in China. Many Qwen models are open source and offer an alternative to those developed in Silicon Valley.

Switzerland takes a different approach. Its Apertus model is a Swiss-developed large language model that openly shares information about its training data, code, and development process. In the Swiss canton of Ticino, it powers an in-house translation service for sensitive government documents without relying on commercial AI providers. The priority here is greater control over how the technology is used, rather than simply choosing the most powerful AI model.
Less a switch, more a dial

There are limits, however. As the Stanford researchers point out, commercial products marketed as “sovereign AI” may still rely on foreign providers. Even models that can be freely adapted still need chips, electricity, and skilled people.

If sovereignty means owning every part of the AI technology stack, almost no country qualifies. But if it means maintaining control when circumstances change, the picture looks different. What matters is whether countries have meaningful choices.

Can they switch suppliers without disrupting essential services? Can they enforce their own laws and adapt AI technologies to local languages, priorities, and needs? These questions reveal more about a country’s sovereignty than simply counting how many chips, data centres, or AI models it owns.

Sovereignty then looks less like a switch and more like a dial. For the UK, the real test will be whether its Sovereign AI Unit gives the country greater freedom to choose and adapt AI technologies as the programme develops.
“Sovereign AI” will probably continue to mean different things to different governments. But the label itself tells us little about how much control a country actually has.

articles.title: Werewolf mice, ghostly frogs and cockroach zombies: the animal versions of our Halloween horrors
articles.author: Alex Dittrich, Senior Lecturer in Zoology, Nottingham Trent University
paras: Around this time of year, elaborate decorations featuring ghosts, vampires, zombies, witches and werewolves adorn front doors, gardens and shop windows across the country.
But you may be surprised to hear that in the animal world, there are many real-life creatures with similar tendencies to these fictional characters of our Halloween nightmares.

The southern grasshopper mouse (Onychomys torridus) howls at the moon to defend its territory and attract mates, a little like werewolves in films. These nocturnal rodents stand up on their hind legs, point their nose upwards, and produce high-pitched sounds.

Grasshopper mice are voracious carnivores, preying upon scorpions, beetles, grasshoppers, and even other mice. They are also immune to the stings of their favourite food – the bark scorpion (Centruroides sculpturatus). Grasshopper mice can block the chemical pathway that transmits the signal from the venom, essentially numbing themselves to the pain. They then bite off the scorpion’s tail, rendering their prey defenseless to their fate.
These little rodents are so formidable that they will unhesitatingly attack anything that is appropriately sized and considered to be food, even if it might be dangerous.

Small mammals, like grasshopper mice, play crucial ecological roles in their ecosystems. For example, through digging their burrows, they can act as ecosystem engineers (species that modify the environment) creating microhabitats for other species.

The emerald jewel wasp (Ampulex compressa) is a stunningly beautiful and ecologically important species. Not only do they act as casual pollinators for a range of plant species, they are also an essential biocontrol; an organism that controls the population of a pest species.

Over millions of years they have evolved the morbid ability to sting cockroaches and turn them into compliant zombies upon which they lay their eggs. When these eggs hatch, the larvae devour the zombified cockroach from the inside out.

Small birds called oxpeckers (Buphagus species) and large ungulates (hoofed mammals) were considered to have a mutually beneficial relationship. When these birds removed pesky ticks and other parasites from their mammalian companions, they were rewarded with a quick, tasty meal. Oxpeckers are often spotted travelling around on the backs of these larger animals.

However, research has highlighted that this relationship may be more complicated than previously thought. Oxpeckers will pick at open wounds to consume blood and flesh – inflicting injuries, preventing wound-healing, and increasing the risk of infection in their hosts.

Witches are well known for creating magical potions but some insects do this too. Bombardier beetles can blast would-be predators with explosive chemicals discharged from their abdomens at temperatures of 100°C. They do this by mixing hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide within their bodies in a small reaction chamber – their cauldron, if you will – to create this explosion.

Some other insects use chemicals not as a defence mechanism, but to woo a mate. This isn’t an elixir of love, but instead the combination of a chemical and an enzyme (Luciferin and luciferase) that causes a beautiful, if slightly eerie, glow.

The fireflies of the family Lampyridae are actually beetles, whose males flash these colours enthusiastically to attract a waiting female from the undergrowth. Beauty and intrigue aside, fireflies are useful throughout their native range. As larvae they feed on many soft-bodied invertebrates, preventing pest outbreaks and maintaining maintaining a natural equilibrium of species in the soil and leaf litter.
Some frogs in the family Centrolenidae are so translucent, or ghost-like, that they have become known as glass frogs.

Found in the tropical forests of Central and South America, these extraordinary frogs spend much of their lives in the trees and play an important role in the ecosystem. They help regulate insect populations through predation and act as prey for a variety of other species, including in aquatic food webs as tadpoles inhabiting streams. In many ways, they occupy multiple levels of the rainforest ecosystem, linking both terrestrial and freshwater environments.

Come Halloween, many people embellish their houses with plastic skeletons and toilet-paper clad mummies. One insect does a similar thing – the aptly named bone-house wasp (Deuteragenia ossarium). Known for hunting another Halloween favourite, the spider, it decorates the nests it makes for its young with a pile of ant corpses. This morbid tableau provides sensory camouflage for the nest, keeping intruders well away.

All these species are important components of their ecosystems – from keeping pest populations in check or being prey themselves for other animals, to acting as ecological indicators allowing us to monitor environmental changes. Ecological indicator species are key species within ecosystems that help us understand more about how our impact on the planet is affecting other species. Animals respond to different things in the environment, so their populations and behaviours can indicate whether the environment is changing for the better or worse.

These animals may have some rather terrifying tendencies, but unlike the fantasy characters of our horror-film nightmares, they don’t disappear after All Hallows’ Eve. They also have real environmental benefits that endure.

articles.title: Scientists map a distant planet’s atmosphere for the first time – and it’s lopsided
articles.author: Hannah Wakeford, Associate professor, University of Bristol
paras: When scientists study exoplanets, planets orbiting stars other than the Sun, they often lack three-dimensional information. For example, general mathematical relationships are used to estimate a planet’s radius, even though that distance may be different depending on where it is measured.

Similar principles apply to measuring the atmosphere of an exoplanet, which often blurs all the features around the planet into one average spectrum. A spectrum is the record of how starlight filters through the atmosphere.
Dr David Grant, at the University of Bristol, and I have developed a new method called “transmission strings” to map the structure of the atmosphere of these distant alien worlds.

By analysing data from the largest and most powerful telescope in space, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), we have, for the first time, mapped the changing shape of an exoplanet atmosphere. The results, published in Nature Astronomy, revealed a planetary atmosphere that was asymmetric – with one side more extended than the other.

In this new research study, led by Dr Lili Alderson at Cornell University in Ithaca, US, we looked at Wasp-17b, which orbits a star some 1,300 light years from Earth. It falls into a category of planet called a hot Jupiter, a giant gas world that orbits close to its host star – and therefore experiences very high temperatures. Wasp-17b’s skewed shape reveals how intense heat and supersonic winds influence the atmosphere.

The transmission strings method involves tracking the planet as it passes in front of its star (or transits) from our point of view on Earth. As this happened, our team captured the composition of light around the edge of the planet’s atmosphere, or limb, from different angles.

As the transit begins and ends (stages known as ingress and egress, respectively) it is possible to obtain spatial information about the planet. This is possible because the ingress and egress is the period of time where the planet is just passing the edge of the star and is not fully in front of its disk.

During ingress and egress, which lasts roughly 31 minutes in total for Wasp-17b, light is only shining through small segments of the atmosphere. At these stages, it is possible to get greater spatial resolution – to measure the extent of the atmosphere with a greater level of detail – than when light is shining through the whole limb of the planet, as it does during the middle phase of the transit. This is illustrated in our artist’s impression at the top of this article.

The transmission strings method fits the ingress and egress measurements with a series of different shapes for the planet’s atmosphere. Our team then compared these with a perfectly circular planet using a series of mathematical functions to determine the best fit. Traditional mathematical modelling extracts a spectrum of light only as an average across the entire limb.
Hot Jupiter planets like Wasp-17b are tidally locked to their star. This means that one side is permanently facing the star, while the other faces the darkness of space.

This drives winds of thousands of miles per hour as the atmosphere moves from the hot to the cold side. The winds transport the heat first across the evening side, then over the nightside where they cool down, and finally over the morning onto the dayside where the atmosphere is heated again and repeats this journey.

The hotter the air, the more inflated a planet’s atmosphere will be. Rather than assuming the atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows astronomers to measure different distances from the centre to the edge of the planet.
We are then able to go around the edge of the planet and measure this changing inflation of the atmosphere, and therefore the changing temperature of the air that makes it up.

Importantly, these first observations implementing the transmission strings method find that the atmospheric chemical composition and temperature shifts match well to theoretical models of the planet.
The atmosphere of Wasp-17b is physically more inflated on the hot side than the cold side, with a smooth transition in temperature over the pole of the planet.
These findings for Wasp-17b are part of a large study of the planet that have previously revealed clouds made of quartz in the planet’s atmosphere.
The Wasp-17b data, from a team led by Professor Nikole Lewis at Cornell University and I, should help astronomers recreate a full map of an exoplanet’s atmosphere from empirical observational data.
This successful demonstration of transmission strings on Wasp-17b not only fulfils this goal but also paves the way for mapping many more exoplanets.

The process is starting to differentiate conditions across exoplanet latitudes, beyond just day and night sides, and providing a first step towards mapping weather-scale patterns in exoplanet climates.

Hannah Wakeford is an Associate Professor at the University of Bristol and receives funding from UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) under the UK government’s Horizon Europe funding guarantee formerly ERC Starting Grant (grant number EP/Y006313/1). articles.title: Falcon 9 ushered in the modern space economy – retiring it could leave the industry vulnerable
articles.author: Mojtaba Akhavan-Tafti, Research Associate Professor, Climate and Space Sciences and Engineering, University of Michigan
paras: More than 50% of the nearly 330 spaceflights to low Earth orbit in 2025 were done on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Falcon 9 is much smaller than SpaceX’s flashy Starship rocket, but for the past 16 years it has been a reliable choice for launching satellites to orbit.

It has carried payloads ranging from Earth-imaging sensors feeding smartphone map apps to environmental monitoring satellites that track wildfires. It has also launched the crew capsule that ferries astronauts to the International Space Station.
In late 2026, reports came out that SpaceX is shuffling its staff in an attempt to focus its resources on developing and commercializing Starship, while phasing out the Falcon 9.

At face value, this sounds like routine news; after all, companies shuffle resources all the time. But as a space scientist, I believe that retiring this rocket threatens to suffocate the commercial space industry that it helped bring to life – unless the public and private sectors step up their efforts to fill the gap Falcon 9’s retirement has created.

Since its inception in 2002, SpaceX has broadened access to space. In 2006, while facing the looming retirement of the space shuttle, NASA searched for a private alternative to resupply the International Space Station. The agency awarded companies contracts, and SpaceX’s award helped kick-start the development of Falcon 9.

Despite multiple near-bankruptcy setbacks, Falcon 9 made its inaugural test flight in 2010, followed by sending the SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule to its first docking at the International Space Station in 2012.

The real turning point came in 2015 with the first successful landing of a Falcon 9 booster. The booster is the rocket’s main first stage. It houses fuel tanks and nine main engines. It provides the primary thrust off the launchpad but detaches from the rest of the rocket shortly after. Landing the booster meant SpaceX could recover and refly this component and dramatically slash launch costs.

In the meantime, Boeing, the other NASA contract awardee, struggled with budget overruns and operational delays. Some of SpaceX’s other competitors, such as Blue Origin, pivoted toward suborbital space tourism. As a result, Falcon 9 did more than just capture the market. It effectively became the market.
A booming industry teetering on the edge

SpaceX’s affordable and frequent access to space helped to breathe life into a booming space economy. It allowed startups with creative new business models to send their satellites to orbit, such as TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup exploring hosting data centers in orbit. It empowered governments around the world to dramatically expand their operations in space, including governments relying on SpaceX’s secured communication platform, named Starshield.

Then came the operational shift. In July 2026, accounts from prospective commercial customers and satellite operators revealed that SpaceX had begun turning away Falcon 9 customers to focus its resources on the more capable Starship rocket.

Almost overnight, the announcement threatened to freeze the pipeline of launches the market relied on. Those who can afford it are paying extra to secure the few remaining slots on Falcon 9, while others are scrambling to find alternative launch opportunities. While European customers are generally flocking to the European Space Agency’s Ariane 6 rocket, others are booking slots on upcoming medium-lift rockets, such as Rocket Lab’s Neutron rocket.

SpaceX is contractually obligated to continue Falcon 9 flights for NASA’s International Space Station crew rotations and other national security payloads. However, the rest of the space industry is now forced to buy into SpaceX’s Starship bet. There simply is no operational alternative today that can match Falcon 9’s combination of high launch cadence, affordable pricing and proven flight heritage for medium-class payloads.
National security vulnerability

When a single company is put in charge of controlling the gate to space, its internal corporate decisions can make or break an industry. That also makes the company a potential single point of failure, where a setback by a single vendor would paralyze the entire space economy.

The U.S. has dealt with this type of national security dilemma before. In the 1900s, Standard Oil owned critical oil production infrastructure, pipelines and railroads. Controlling critical pipeline networks gave the company unprecedented power to set transport terms, prioritize its own shipments and restrict pipeline access for independent oil producers. This structure meant competitors had no viable alternative transport routes. Ultimately, this forced the U.S. government to intervene because internal Standard Oil corporate decisions dictated market dynamics.

Standard Oil had become the gatekeeper to the free flow of oil. By addressing that potential single point of failure, the U.S. government nudged an industry to redefine itself, which led to its accelerated growth.
Customers forced to pay up
SpaceX took huge technical and financial bets on the success of Falcon 9. They paid off and led to SpaceX’s market dominance.

But now SpaceX wants to do it again, with the promise that Starship would help further reduce the cost of getting to space. Their vision is grand, but what happens if Starship experiences delays? What happens to companies who relied on Falcon 9?

As SpaceX shifts focus, competing launch providers will likely rush to take advantage of this market opportunity and offer rides to customers being turned away by SpaceX, but at a steep premium. The customers also face the burden of reconfiguring their satellites to fit on another rocket.

This sudden market shift has been a wake-up call, one that I believe will cost the industry and add significant uncertainty to market dynamics in a few years. But it also offers the market an opportunity to correct course by filling the gap that Falcon 9’s retirement has created.

Over the past two decades, NASA has successfully delivered on its mandate to create a rocket-launch marketplace. To achieve this, NASA fundamentally shifted from operating government-owned hardware to buying fixed-price services. This meant that NASA became a reliable anchor customer whose contracts spurred competition among commercial providers.
While this model proved that routine, low-cost space access was achievable, various technical and business challenges allowed the marketplace to become dominated by a single vendor.

Moving forward, NASA and other public agencies can work together to strategically distribute the payloads they need to launch across commercial rockets built by other companies. These government contracts can help these companies improve and validate their emerging rocket programs. Satellite customers can design standardized payloads that work across multiple types of rockets, so they don’t rely on one launch provider.

NASA can also maintain its dedicated launch assistance programs. Subsidizing these slots would allow smaller institutions, such as academia and nonprofit organizations, to avoid competing on the open market against large companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin that launch satellites regularly. These programs help smaller institutions that may not have the funds to directly buy their own spot on a rocket get their payload to space. These payloads are often used to give students experience and help train the next generation of space workers exploring the cosmos.

articles.title: Drones could help weather forecasters more accurately predict winter storms
articles.author: Declan Finney, Senior Research Fellow in Cloud Physics, University of Leeds
paras: Weather drones are being tested to help update forecasts of extreme weather more quickly, and could help us prepare earlier for upcoming winter storms.

With an unprecedented El Niño increasing the chance of storms and wet weather in Europe this winter, meteorologists will be looking at new and developing tools to help them forecast as accurately as possible.
The ability of new types of weather drones to collect more information ahead of incoming bad weather has already attracted the attention of financial traders.

Energy traders have to buy and sell electricity produced from sources like wind and solar farms. They need to judge the supply and demand as quickly as possible. This means they need updates to weather forecasts so they can predict when clouds might shade solar panels, or if an approaching storm could increase wind turbine generation.

US researchers have recently highlighted that the ability of drones to collect information on air pressure and wind speed, for instance, in real time is proving useful for forecasting extreme weather events faster.

Meanwhile, UK researchers are pushing the technology further by using drones to collect valuable data inside clouds. Clouds are fundamental to many weather effects, including rain, fog, lightning, hail and extreme winds.

In 2024, the World Meteorological Organisation hosted its first demonstration of weather drones. These drones measured temperature and wind speed, and focused on the lowest few kilometres of the atmosphere.

This use of drones is being developed with the expectation that they can be used as part of a network of drone stations by meteorological agencies, to complement traditional networks of weather stations.

These drones can be deployed remotely from a dock, allowing routine measurement of the lower atmosphere to inform weather forecasts. This is similar to how weather balloons currently operate. Drones, however, have the potential to provide data at much higher frequency, and more quickly. Data could be collected hourly or more often, and with less waste such as lost weather balloon equipment.

A new research project, Drone Observation Of Clouds (DOOC), led by the University of Leeds, is working out if new kinds of measurement could become part of weather forecasting in the future. They are looking at measuring the most uncertain component of weather and climate, clouds.

Between June and November 2026 DOOC has been flying and collecting measurements at a site in Yorkshire, UK. Leeds-based drone operator, Menapia, has collaborated with University of Leeds to obtain permission to fly in an unusually narrow column of air up to 1,600 metres.

That small section of airspace enables a weather drone to measure temperature, humidity, wind and cloud particles at all heights between the ground and 1,600 metres. At only 30m wide, this narrow piece of airspace only makes sense for a rotor drone that can ascend perfectly vertically.

A particle counter is mounted on the drone and can determine the size and concentration of cloud droplets. It has been developed and tested for almost a decade, honing it to be suitable for drone-based measurement.
The DOOC project will build on recent forecasting advances at the UK Met Office. UK forecasts now use a much more detailed representation of cloud physics to make forecasts more accurate.

Drone-based measurements of weather and clouds could offer the next breakthroughs in the rapidly growing field of AI weather forecasting. AI weather forecasting leans more heavily on data than traditional forecasting methods. So, the collection of routine observations of the atmosphere has become more important than ever.

As US researchers are also finding, one of the greatest challenges is how to work with regulators to enable drone operation for research alongside traditional air users, as well as commercial and military drone users.
Scientists are arguing for new infrastructure investment and regulatory support to make the most of this developing drone technology.

Drone observations have the potential to greatly benefit wider society through the improved weather forecasts, which will mean the ability to prepare better for upcoming extreme weather earlier, and potentially put protection in place.

articles.title: What is artificial general intelligence – and is it already here?
articles.author: Waqas Ali, Lecturer in Business Management and Research, Faculty of Arts, Business, and Social Sciences, University of Wolverhampton
paras: OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, recently suggested that its advanced model, known as GPT-6 Astra, could mark the arrival of something called artificial general intelligence, or AGI.

If AI itself is often defined as the ability to simulate human intelligence, OpenAI defines AGI as an AI system that outperforms humans at most economically valuable work – to be better at the majority of digital and cognitive tasks a human can perform. This includes tasks such as writing computer code, organisational activities or managing projects.

For now, at least, it excludes work that involves physical labour, such as agriculture or construction. Though the integration of AI with robotics means such sectors of industry may not be the exclusive domain of humans forever.

This definition by OpenAI focuses on breadth of competency by an AI system. However, other experts maintain that AGI will be characterised by additional cognitive leaps beyond present-day AI models. For example, Demis Hassabis, founder of Google DeepMind, has said that AGI should be able to do “pretty much any cognitive task that humans can do”.

This definition makes AGI more about brilliance and a bit less about depth. Yann LeCun, former chief AI scientist at Meta, believes the term AGI itself is flawed and should be replaced by “human-level AI”.
These represent snapshots from a vigorous ongoing debate over when AGI will arrive and how to recognise it.

Venturebeat magazine reported Brockman acknowledging this at a closed press briefing about GPT-6 Astra in September when he said: “When we started OpenAI, we kind of thought that there was going to be this well-defined moment that everyone would recognise … it hasn’t played out like that.”

But he added: “For me personally, I do think we’re there.” Just a few days after Brockman made his comments, the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, called in an essay titled: “We must pace the frontier” for the AI industry to slow down the pace of its development. Within hours of this essay being published, both Sam Altman and Elon Musk signalled their agreement.
So is Brockman right about AGI being here? The evidence still points in more than one direction and is therefore inconclusive.

The clearest shift with GPT-6 Astra is in how people use it. Earlier models needed detailed instructions at each step. Astra is built for longer jobs where the user sets a goal and some boundaries, and the model works out the sequence itself.

OpenAI’s demonstrations showed the frontier model handling several unrelated tasks at once. The company presents this as moving past the pattern in which a human supplies the next instruction every time.
That is a real change, and it is the part most users will notice first.

One of the benchmarks show that Astra scored 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3, a test that places an AI agent in unfamiliar interactive games with no instructions and measures how efficiently it works out the rules.

OpenAI estimates that the average human scored 48% when asked to work out the same unfamiliar games. The detail matters here, however. ARC Prize, which runs the benchmark, reported that Astra’s best score through the shared “harness” it gives every model was 62.7%. A harness is a kind of software operating system, or physical environment, within which the AI system works. ARC Prize provides Astra with this software harness.

The 99.9% came from a different harness, built by OpenAI for Astra, which preserves the AI model’s reasoning between requests. Essentially, Astra did better when it was able to reuse previous work and wasn’t “starting from scratch” between requests in terms of its reasoning.

Independent evaluators disagree about how much of an advance GPT-6 Astra represents on its predecessor. The independent research institute Epoch AI places it right at the frontier, alongside other cutting-edge AI models such as Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3 and GPT-5.5 Pro. The independent analysis company Artificial Analysis did not rate it as being radically ahead of its predecessor – GPT-5.6 Sol.

Toby Walsh, an AI researcher at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, described the intelligence in frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra and others as “still today very jagged”, telling Al Jazeera that there are simple things that even the best AI models do poorly.

On September 8 2026, OpenAI published a claimed solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven Millennium Prize problems in mathematics. This has often been reported as Astra’s work. It was not. OpenAI says the proof came from an unreleased internal model, significantly more capable than Astra, running roughly 10,000 AI agents (AI models that perform tasks in response to human instructions) in parallel for about 88 hours.
Astra’s contribution was the formalisation and verification afterwards, which took a further 17 hours. The proof has not yet been checked by the mathematical community.

Amodei’s September essay calling for an AI slowdown remains the strongest recent statement about the risks of frontier models. He wrote that within six to 12 months, a swarm of agents could be capable of taking over the internet with a persistent botnet. This could lead to the catastrophic failure of key systems and would cause damage possibly running into hundreds of billions of dollars.
It is worth examining Amodei’s warnings. Anthropic’s September threat report sets out examples of how AI is already being used in alarming ways.

According to the Anthropic report, a group in northern Yemen recently used Claude code to build guidance software for rockets and a missile. Russian and Chinese operators automated espionage work. A single French-speaking individual built used AI to build a software platform that made personal information about people affiliated with a targeted political movement searchable online. In each case, a human chose the targets and the model supplied the labour.
That is a narrow capability applied at speed and scale under human direction. It is serious, but it is not a description of general intelligence.

Capability and general intelligence are separate things, and they call for different responses. Amodei’s proposed response is to slow frontier development while expanding independent evaluation and coordinating safety standards across countries. A genuinely general system would raise questions that those measures are not designed to answer.

GPT-6 Astra does not settle whether AGI has arrived. Instead, it exposes why that question is becoming harder to answer. Intelligence is increasingly a property of an AI system comprising a model, memory, tools and agents, rather than of a model tested in isolation.
On the narrower question of whether these systems can now cause serious harm, the people running the companies have said plainly that they definitely can.

articles.title: The hydrogen atom: the raw material of the universe barely exists on Earth – now we’ve made it in a flask
articles.author: Roopender Kumar, Lecturer in Organic Chemistry and Chemical Biology, UCL
paras: What do you see when you look up at the night sky? While everyone may have a different answer, the truth is that almost everything out there is hydrogen. The first element in the periodic table is by far the most abundant substance in the cosmos. It’s the fuel of stars and the raw material from which the heavier elements were forged over billions of years. Even the Sun is, at its core, a furnace for fusing hydrogen atoms together.

Despite this abundance, the hydrogen atom has been almost completely inaccessible in the chemistry lab for over a century. It’s a strange irony; physicists have explored the hydrogen atom for as long as modern science has existed.

In fact, the hydrogen atom is the most studied and well understood system in the history of physics. Take Niels Bohr’s famous model of atomic structure – it was built on the hydrogen atom. Erwin Schrödinger solved his famous quantum wave equation for it first. And when Paul Dirac merged quantum mechanics, the theory of particles and atoms, with Albert Einstein’s special relativity, it revealed a lot of the fine structure of the element.
For synthetic chemists, who build chemical compounds and molecules, it has been almost out of reach – until now.

To be clear, I’m not talking about the hydrogen molecule that comes in a gas canister, which consists of two hydrogen atoms bound together. And I’m not talking about the hydrogen ion (which has an extra electron) or the proton (a particle which makes up the atomic nucleus of the hydrogen atom). What I am talking about is the lone, simple hydrogen atom: a single electron orbiting a single proton.

This single, unpaired electron makes it what chemists call a radical; the most fundamental reactive species in all of chemistry. Until recently, generating it required conditions so extreme that it was simply not a tool synthetic chemists could use.

The Insights section is committed to high-quality longform journalism. Our editors work with academics from many different backgrounds who are tackling a wide range of societal and scientific challenges.

In 1912, Irving Langmuir, an American chemist at General Electric, who would win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1932, became the first scientist to temporarily make atomic hydrogen. He did this by heating molecular hydrogen over a tungsten filament to above 1,700°C, splitting hydrogen gas into individual hydrogen atoms. When these atoms combine together at a cooler metal surface, they release enormous amounts of energy, producing temperatures of 3,400°C to 4,000°C.
In fact, this heat proved sufficient to weld tungsten, the most heat-resistant of all metals. For decades, this method was one of the most potent industrial welding processes.

And progress continued. In 1922, James Franck, a German-American physicist who would later win the Nobel Prize in Physics, discovered that mercury atoms exposed to ultraviolet light at 254 nanometres could absorb that energy and then transfer it to hydrogen molecules, breaking them apart into atoms.

This process, called mercury photosensitisation, was based on fundamental physics, however. It wasn’t intended to be used to do chemistry. And while it worked, it required toxic mercury vapour, the use of which is heavily regulated, and specialised ultraviolet lamps.

The first chemist to recognise that hydrogen atoms might be genuinely useful as synthetic reagents (artificial substances that can cause, control or assist chemical reactions) was Robert Crabtree at Yale University. In a 1991 paper in the Journal of the American Chemical Society, he demonstrated that James’ mercury photosensitisation could be adapted.

The hydrogen atoms that were created in the process could be used to break double carbon bonds (where two carbon atoms are bound together by four bonding electrons instead of two) in organic compounds such as olefins, which are a building block of plastics. This was an important work, as it showed that the hydrogen atom could be successfully used to do chemistry, such as discovering new drugs.

But his method still required toxic mercury vapour and a specialised UV lamp. Critically, it also failed to work in liquid solutions, requiring vapour instead. Synthetic chemistry, however, is done in solutions (it’s easier to mix components in a liquid). So even after Crabtree, the hydrogen atom remained out of reach to synthetic chemists.

My laboratory at University College London set out to close that gap. I wanted to know if it was possible to create atomic hydrogen at room temperature, in a liquid solution, using ordinary laboratory equipment. Surprisingly, after all these years, the answer appears to be yes. We’ve now published our results in the Journal of the American Chemical Society.

I began this work alone in my laboratory. But I was lucky that Nils Flodén, a postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Colloids and Interfaces in Potsdam, Germany, soon joined me as a collaborator.

Our method uses two inexpensive, commercially available chemicals: hydrazine (a molecule consisting of two nitrogen atoms and four hydrogen atoms) and thiophenol (consisting of a mix of carbon, hydrogen and sulphur). When mixed together and exposed to near-ultraviolet light from a standard LED lamp, these generate atomic hydrogen at only 30°C. The result truly amazed me. We used no toxic mercury vapour, no extreme temperatures. All we needed was a flask, a lamp and two reagents available from any chemical supplier.

When hydrazine and thiophenol are mixed, they form an intermediate substance that absorbs near-ultraviolet light. This triggers an electron to move places, producing a short-lived, highly unstable species that rapidly falls apart, releasing a hydrogen atom in the process.

But our goal was not creating a fleeting hydrogen atom that quickly disappears – we wanted to use it to do chemistry. And amazingly, we discovered that the hydrogen atom we’d created was free to react with organic molecules in ways that are crucial in many chemical experiments, such as adding it onto double bonds of carbon to form less reactive (more stable) single bond, and removing halogens (such as flourine, iodine and chlorine).

The precise nature of the unstable intermediate is still being investigated, but our current evidence points toward a species physicists call a Rydberg radical, in which an electron occupies an unusually large and diffuse orbit around the molecule before the whole thing breaks apart. In fact, our hypothesis is inspired by the work of Nobel Laureate Gerhard Herzerbeg on something called a Rydberg radical of ammonia (ammonium radical), which was published in 1981.

How do we know we have made a hydrogen atom? We used something called EPR spin-trapping, consisting of a chemical net that can ultimately catch short-lived radicals that we can identify by their magnetic fingerprint. And this revealed that hydrogen atoms had formed at the end. When we used a version of hydrazine where the hydrogen atoms were replaced by the heavier isotope deuterium (a hydrogen atom with a neutron added to its nucleus), we caught deuterium atoms instead, exactly as predicted. This EPR spectroscopy was performed with Alberto Collauto at Imperial College London.
A molecular stopwatch called a radical clock further supported the mechanism. Every experiment pointed in the same direction.

Having atomic hydrogen available as a practical reagent in a liquid solution could open possibilities that were not there before. The most immediate application is hydrogenation: adding hydrogen atoms across a carbon-carbon double bond to break them up. This is one of the most important reactions in pharmaceutical manufacturing, used to make drugs ranging from cholesterol treatments to antivirals.

Currently, most industrial hydrogenation requires metals such as palladium, rhodium or iridium to act as catalysts, often under high-pressure hydrogen gas. But there’s a limited global supply of such metals, making them expensive and strictly regulated in drug products.

Our hydrogen atom method requires none of them. It is metal-free, operates at atmospheric pressure and close to room temperature. But could it actually be used in drug manufacturing? We managed to use our method, without disturbing other chemical groups, to reduce double bonds in a derivative of fluoxetine (an SSRI), in terpenoids (compounds found in fragrances and flavours) and in an amino acid. This can help make drugs more stable in the body and less reactive.
We also demonstrated hydrodehalogenation: the selective removal of halogen atoms from organic molecules. This is often done in medicinal chemistry for fine-tuning drug candidates.

As for other applications, atomic hydrogen is already used industrially for cleaning semiconductor surfaces in microchip manufacturing, where it removes naturally occurring oxide layers that reduce device performance. Those processes currently require plasma equipment and ultra-high vacuum conditions.
Whether our mild solution could eventually offer an alternative is currently unknown. But for the first time, it is an actual alternative worth exploring.

How did I come up with the idea in the first place? It grew from two parallel interests. I have long been fascinated by hydrogen as a clean fuel and the challenge of storing it conveniently. After all, hydrogen has been the fuel of the universe for 13 billion years.

At the same time, I was working on developing new synthetic methods in organic chemistry. About half a decade ago, it struck me that, despite decades of exploration, the reactive hydrogen atom itself has remained almost entirely unexplored as a synthetic tool. Finding a practical way to generate it could be useful for hydrogen storage and beyond. This was the starting point.
This was ultimately a dream project. The more I thought about it, the harder it was to let it go. At some point, it practically consumed me.

It’s been a long journey for me. In 2010, as a student from a small village in northern India, I had the opportunity to travel to Berlin and work in the lab of Hans Ulrich Reissig of Freie Universität Berlin, the first research laboratory I had ever set foot in. The paper is dedicated to him on the occasion of his 77th birthday. It was where I first understood, with absolute certainty, that chemistry was my calling.
It may have taken a century to bring atomic hydrogen into the synthetic chemist’s laboratory, but we hope it will prove to be worth the wait.

I was fortunate to receive a Royal Society Research Grant (RG\R1\251599), which supported the purchase of key instruments for the laboratory. But there was no grant to support a researcher dedicated to this project. I am an optimist by nature, and there is a bright side. When there is no funded researcher, there is no funder to tell you what to work on. No review panel would have funded a newly appointed lecturer to chase the smallest radical in the universe with no preliminary data and no obvious path to a clinical application. I know this because I tried: more than a dozen applications, none successful. And so, in a peculiar way, the absence of a grant was also a kind of freedom. What made all the difference, was the generosity of an exceptional collaborator - Nils Flodén who believed in the project and gave his time, expertise, and intellectual energy without any obligation to do so. Science, at its best, is exactly that.

articles.title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky – this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
articles.author: David Hu, Professor of Mechanical Engineering and Biology, Adjunct Professor of Physics, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: Here’s a bit of a riddle for you: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects?

The medical term for earwax is cerumen, based on keros, the Greek word for beeswax. People have been pondering earwax since ancient times. Ancient hygiene kits including picks and spoons to remove earwax have been found in archaeological sites worldwide.

Even today, it remains a perpetual question: to remove or not to remove your earwax? The answer: Don’t do it. The general medical belief is that ears are self-cleaning, and earwax brings benefits such as lubricating the ear canal, fighting infection and acting like a sticky net to trap debris before it reaches the eardrum. By poking in there you can accidentally make matters worse, pushing wax deeper or scratching your delicate ear canal.

Cerumen impaction – or blocked earwax – affects about a fifth of the American population, leading to 12 million patient visits per year. Blockages are worsened by daily activities such as wearing earbuds or hearing aids.

Another common problem with ears is wedged debris. For children, much of this is self-inflicted, in the form of items such as Legos or erasers. But for many adults who have something stuck in their ear, the debris is insects, such as ants, beetles, flies or cockroaches.

While rare for the average person, insects in the ear occurred with such frequency over the years that physicians began to wonder whether earwax evolved as a natural barrier for insects. But how would such a barrier work?

To answer this question, my Ph.D. student David Ancalle led experiments with earwax and insects. We teamed up with Yuhang Hu and her student Donjing He, experts in the behavior of soft solids such as hydrogels. As mechanical engineers, we wanted to focus on the physics rather than the chemistry of earwax.
Our research, published in the journal Soft Matter, shows that earwax can, in fact, stop insects without the use of dangerous chemicals.
Watching ants encounter earwax
To do experiments, we needed voluminous amounts of earwax.

Initially we obtained earwax from deceased mammals such as pigs, sheep and rabbits. Eventually we turned to our friends and family. A person has only a grain of rice’s worth of earwax in each ear. Due to a mutation in a single gene, East Asians have dry, flaky earwax, while people of African or European descent have wet, squishy earwax.

To simulate an ant climbing into an ear canal, we used a glass beaker with its rim coated in earwax. Ants, like many insects, are climbing specialists, capable of traveling across many kinds of surfaces. To climb rough surfaces, ants have spikes on their feet, like mountain climbers do, that helps them grasp onto ridges and cracks. For smooth surfaces, ants unfurl wet suction cups, which can support 60 times their body weight on smooth glass.
Watching ants trying to climb earwax showed us how strange a substance it really is. Rough earwax slowed them down, but with their claws they made progress.
But as soon as ants tried to climb smooth earwax, they fell immediately.
From these experiments, we concluded that earwax had anti-stick properties when in contact with the insects’ feet.

We next conducted experiments with ants crawling through an earwax-coated tunnel, more similar in size to a human ear canal. As the ants attempted to travel through the tunnel, earwax stuck to them. Once coated, they groomed furiously, unwilling to walk until they had removed as much as possible. Even after several minutes of effort, the ants still had earwax sticking to hard-to-reach places.

So, earwax is a paradoxical material: It is simultaneously slippery, thanks to the lipids it contains, but also sticky. Similar to many materials – including ketchup, paint and shampoo – it thins out when it is physically deformed, what physicists call shear-thinning.
Figuring out earwax’s physical properties

The dual qualities of earwax have to do with its unique composition. Earwax is made up of flakes of skin cells held together with a binder. This blend forms a kind of sponge with microscopic holes. When a body overproduces earwax, it heaps up in boulders that ants can easily climb over.

When the substance is smooth, however, ants rely on their wet suction cups. The holes in the earwax absorb the drops produced by the ants, preventing them from attaching. Absorbency makes earwax fundamentally different from commonly used forms of pest control.

In your local store, you will find sticky surfaces such as fly paper or chemicals that kill the insects. Some researchers look to nature to find bio-friendly alternatives to using chemicals; for example, plants have properties that prevent insects from climbing.
From this study, we learned that the ear is also a model for insect repellency. Earwax is made of natural materials but has a structure that prevents ants from sticking to it.

The porosity of earwax also gives it unique properties. We showed it can absorb twice its weight in water yet still cling to the walls of the ear. This water-absorbing ability may help prevent water from accumulating on the delicate eardrum and fend off infections such as swimmer’s ear.
Scientists don’t yet understand the complex relationship between earwax, water and bacteria. Some studies show that earwax kills bacteria, but other studies find that earwax harbors bacteria.

Our experiments showed that earwax is most challenging to insects when similar to the thin layer of earwax maintained by a healthy human body. Wax would accumulate more in human ears if not for two self-cleaning mechanisms. The skin in the ear canal grows outward like a conveyor belt. Over 8-10 weeks, this process – called epithelial migration – pushes the oldest earwax out of the ear.

Simultaneously, earwax dries over time, transforming from a gooey state to a brittle one that readily cracks. Every time you talk or chew, your ear canal deforms, and physicians found that this movement helps to dislodge the drier, older earwax.

As a test of our concept, a member of our team, chemical engineer Rafeen Rahaman, designed an artificial earwax based on the physical structure rather than the chemistry of the earwax. Ants struggled when they touched it, just like when they interacted with natural earwax.

The cost of harvesting natural earwax and our recipe for artificial earwax are not cheap. We don’t foresee our methods replacing insect repellents produced at large scale. But perhaps the concept might inspire new ways to prevent earwax from coating our earbuds or lead to the manufacture of insect control methods using safe formulations.

articles.title: We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth
articles.author: Simon Buechler, Assistant Professor of Finance, Miami University
paras: Data centers require enormous investments: land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure. Yet, once they’re up and running, they tend to employ no more than a few dozen people in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are asking what they will get in return.

Skepticism about the local benefits of data centers is contributing to growing opposition to their construction, from Ohio to Texas. That pushback contributed to delays or cancellations of US$156 billion in proposed data center projects in 2025 alone.

We are professors who study real estate and urban economics, including how large place-based investments shape local economies. So we set out to answer a question at the center of these fights: Do data centers actually create jobs where they are built?

To find out, we teamed up with four colleagues to study what happens to local employment after data centers open. We found that new data centers that opened from 2000-2023 created 1,000 to 1,300 jobs in the counties where they are located, on average. But those jobs, which are for work performed outside data centers rather than inside them, take a few years to appear. They are mostly in industries that support data centers, not in restaurants or shops.
How data centers create local jobs
Data centers can create jobs in at least three ways beyond employing people who work inside them.
First, they can increase demand for local suppliers, from security companies that protect the facilities to electrical contractors that maintain their equipment.
Second, data center employees and workers at these suppliers may spend more money locally, supporting restaurants, stores and other local services.

Third, companies already operating data centers may expand their facilities, while other operators may decide to build nearby. Once a location has the electricity, fiber connections and other infrastructure needed to operate a data center, further investment may become easier.
Tracking data centers and jobs

We assembled detailed information on 1,584 U.S. data centers that opened between 2000 and 2023. For each facility, we recorded its location, opening date and power capacity, which is a standard way to compare facilities of different sizes. We then matched these records with federal data on employment, wages and the number of businesses in each county.

Isolating the effect of data centers isn’t straightforward. Operators don’t choose locations randomly. They look for reliable electricity, fiber connections, available land and friendly local regulations. Those places may already be growing, so new jobs might have appeared even without a data center.

To account for this, we tracked employment in counties that received data centers – such as Loudoun County in Virginia, Berkeley County in South Carolina, Morrow County in Oregon, and others – before and after the operation of the facility began. We then compared those trends with similar counties that did not receive data centers. We also looked at whether larger facilities brought bigger job gains.
Jobs appear, but not immediately

During the first two years after a county’s first data center opened, we found little change in employment outside construction. After that, jobs begin to grow. Three to five years after a center opened, we found that these counties had roughly 1,000 to 1,300 additional nonconstruction jobs than comparable counties without data centers.
Bigger investments brought bigger employment gains. Five years after new data center capacity is installed, each additional megawatt is associated with about 7.4 more nonconstruction local jobs.

Part of that gain, however, reflects further expansion. Each megawatt installed is associated with another 1.7 megawatts of capacity over the following years. Once that later growth is counted, our estimates work out to about 2.7 nonconstruction jobs per megawatt of eventual data center capacity. A large 100-megawatt facility, for example, would be correlated with roughly 275 additional local jobs outside the data center itself.
Jobs are not where you might expect
The types of jobs created help explain what is happening.

Employment gains are concentrated in transportation and warehousing, professional and technical services and real estate. These industries may serve or benefit directly from data centers or from the investment and infrastructure they bring.
By contrast, we found little evidence of job growth in restaurants, stores and other local services.

We also found that more data center investment tends to follow in the same county. Most often, the companies already operating in a county expand their facilities. Other companies generally don’t move into that same area to build new data centers.
Jobs are only one side of the equation

Our study has limits. It covers data centers that opened through 2023, before the current wave of massive facilities were built to power AI. Larger data centers do not necessarily create proportionally more jobs, so our findings may not apply to today’s biggest projects.

We also looked only at job gains and did not explore whether data centers are worth their cost to local communities. These facilities consume large amounts of electricity and water, can generate noise and may receive substantial tax breaks from local and state governments. We did not address any of those concerns.

Our findings do show that data centers can create jobs beyond the small number of people working inside their walls. But that does not mean every one of them is a good deal for their local community. And whether those additional jobs justify the costs remains an open question.
